quote: {+Angenäherte+} Berechnung der Anzahl der Lösungen diophantischer Ungleichung [-…-] z. B. $a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots a_nx_n<[-…-]A$
english: Approximate calculation of the number of solutions of Diophantine inequalities, e.g. $a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots a_nx_n<A$.
topic: A list of research questions: reducing the number of parameters in an equation by solving equations of lower order, literature on equation theory in Mathematische Annalen, non-associative or non-commutative composition rules, and approximate counting of solutions of Diophantine inequalities by lattice points in a pyramid.

triage.modern_statement: Given positive real weights a_1,...,a_n and a bound A, estimate N(A), the number of non-negative (or positive) integer vectors (x_1,...,x_n) with a_1x_1+...+a_nx_n < A. Equivalently, count the lattice points in the n-dimensional right-angled simplex (a 'pyramid' or tetrahedron) cut off by this hyperplane. The main term is the volume A^n/(n! a_1...a_n). The real question is how large the error term is, and how it depends on the Diophantine (arithmetic) properties of the a_i. When the a_i are rational, the question becomes Ehrhart theory: the count is a quasi-polynomial in the dilation parameter.
triage.answered_by: No single person settled it. It grew into a whole research area. Hardy and Littlewood (1922) treated n=2, the lattice points of a right-angled triangle, with error terms governed by Diophantine approximation of a_1/a_2. D. C. Spencer extended this to tetrahedra and higher dimensions (J. Math. Phys. 21, 1942). Mordell (1951) linked the count in a tetrahedron to generalized Dedekind sums. Ehrhart theory (1960s onward) gives the exact quasi-polynomial count when the a_i are rational. Work on sharp upper bounds continues today: Yau's conjecture on positive integral points in n-dimensional tetrahedra (Xu and Yau and others) has been proved for small n such as 5 and 6, and lattice-point counts in simplices with algebraic irrational vertices are also still being studied.

evidence.claim: Hardy and Littlewood, 'Some problems of Diophantine approximation: The lattice-points of a right-angled triangle' (Second memoir), Abh. Math. Sem. Hamburg 1 (1922), 211–248. There is also a first memoir in Proc. London Math. Soc. s2-20 (1922), 15–36.
D. C. Spencer, 'The Lattice Points of Tetrahedra', Journal of Mathematics and Physics 21 (1942), 189–197.
'The lattice-points of n-dimensional tetrahedra' (Indagationes Mathematicae, 1975) continues the Hardy–Littlewood line in n dimensions.

Modern work on a sharp estimate of positive integral points in 6-dimensional polyhedra (Yau-type conjecture). It cites Mordell (1951), 'Lattice points in a tetrahedron and generalized Dedekind sums', and Spencer.
Paper on formulas for Dedekind sums and the number of lattice points in tetrahedra Δ(a_1,...,a_n), with a sharp upper estimate.
Recent paper 'Lattice Points in Algebraic Cross-polytopes and Simplices' (Discrete Comput. Geom., 2017). It studies |tP ∩ Z^d| for simplices and cites Hardy–Littlewood.
Ehrhart polynomial of a lattice n-simplex (ERA-AMS 1996). This is the exact-count theory for the rational case.

triage.why: The note is clearly identifiable: it asks how many lattice points lie in the simplex Σ a_i x_i < A, which matches the page summary's 'lattice points in a pyramid'. It is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. The question was taken up and largely answered in the 20th century: the main term is the volume, and the error terms were worked out by Hardy–Littlewood (n=2, 1922), Spencer (tetrahedra, 1942) and Mordell (Dedekind sums, 1951). For rational a_i, Ehrhart theory gives exact formulas. Refinements are still published, including sharp-estimate conjectures of Yau type and results for irrational or algebraic simplices, so the area is active. The verdict is 'solved' only in the sense that the basic question has an established theory. The note is too vague to point to one specific open target, and I found no source connecting Hilbert's note to these later works. Confidence is medium because a search-tool limit stopped me from fetching more detailed statements of the Yau conjecture's current status.
